did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a prophecy about the drought—a severe and prolonged drought affecting the entire land.
The drought also affects the upper classes: the leaders of the people send their young men to look for water, but they return with empty containers and in shame.
Even the doe, which normally protects her young, is forced to abandon it because there is no grass in the field.
Even wild donkeys, animals adapted to the desert, suffer from the drought: they stand on the barren heights, gasp for air, and lose their ability to see because there is no vegetation.
In the midst of the drought, the people confess their sins and ask the LORD to act for the sake of his name, while acknowledging that their rebellions are many.
The people call the LORD the "Hope of Israel"—that is, their hope and savior—but ask why he seems like a stranger or a traveler in the land.
The LORD describes the people as those who love to "wander": their feet do not hold back from wandering, so the LORD does not accept them and remembers their wrongdoing.
According to the LORD’s word, fasting, cries of joy, burnt offerings, and grain offerings will not be accepted in this situation; the punishment will come through sword, famine, and plague.

The LORD makes clear that prophets who promise there will be neither sword nor famine were not sent by him; their prophecies are described as false visions, divination, and the deceit of their own hearts.

At the end of the chapter, it is emphasized that only the LORD can send rain: the worthless gods of the nations cannot bring showers, so the people declare that they hope in the LORD, the Creator of all things.
